results.answer: A binary indexed tree stores at each index k the sum of the original array elements in the range of length p(k)=k&‑k that ends at k, so the prefix [1,k] can be expressed as a union of a few such ranges. To compute sum(1,k) the algorithm repeatedly adds tree[k] to an accumulator and then moves to the next index k ← k − (k&‑k) until k = 0, thereby summing the O(log n) stored ranges that together form the prefix [1,k]【3】【4】.

A segment‑tree query only traverses a path up the tree’s height: the tree has O(log n) levels, and at each level the range can be split into at most two sub‑ranges, so the algorithm visits at most a constant number of nodes per level. Consequently the total number of visited nodes – and thus the query time – is O(log n) [4][5].

The union‑find structure determines that two elements are in the same set by finding each element’s representative and checking whether the representatives are identical (e.g., `same(a,b)` returns `find(a)==find(b)`)【4】【5】

The Z‑algorithm scans the string from left to right, keeping a window [x, y] that is the rightmost segment s[x…y] that matches the prefix of the string. For each new position k it first looks at the previously computed value z[k‑x]; if k + z[k‑x] < y the value can be copied (z[k] = z[k‑x]), otherwise the algorithm extends the match by comparing characters one‑by‑one beyond y and updates the window accordingly — this reuse of earlier Z‑values together with occasional character‑by‑character comparison yields the full Z‑array in linear time [1][3][4].

Topological sorting yields a linear ordering of the graph’s nodes in which every node precedes all nodes reachable from it (i.e., for each edge a→b, a appears before b)【1】. This ordering exists for any directed acyclic graph【1】.

Yes. By precomputing a prefix‑sum (cumulative‑sum) array you can answer any fixed‑range sum with a single subtraction, giving an instant O(1) lookup. A binary indexed (Fenwick) tree is just a dynamic version of that idea when updates are needed【1】【2】.

Jumping to the middle (or using progressively halved jumps) cuts the remaining search region roughly in half at each step, so the number of elements examined grows only with the logarithm of the list size, giving an O(log n) time complexity. Walking through the list one by one examines each element sequentially, which requires O(n) steps, making it much slower for large lists. [2][5]

You can compute a hash value for each piece of text (for example, using polynomial hashing where the hash is a weighted sum of character codes modulo a constant) and then compare the hash values instead of the characters themselves【2】.  
After an O(n) preprocessing that builds prefix hashes, the hash of any substring can be obtained in O(1) time, so equal hash values indicate the texts are probably identical, while different hash values guarantee they differ
Yes. A walk that traverses each connection (edge) exactly once without repetition is called an Eulerian path [1][3].

Pick any node a in the tree, run a depth‑first (or breadth‑first) search to locate the node b that is farthest from a. Then start a second search from b to find the node c that is farthest from b; the pair (b, c) are the two points that are farthest apart, and the distance between them is the tree’s diameter【2】. This two‑search method works because the farthest node from an arbitrary start must be an endpoint of a longest path, and the farthest node from that endpoint gives the opposite endpoint【2】.

Keep a monotonic queue (deque) of the window’s elements. When the window moves, discard from the back any elements larger than the new entry, push the new entry onto the back, and pop the front if its element is no longer inside the window; the element at the front is then the current minimum. This lets you update the minimum in O(1) per step, giving an overall O(n) algorithm [1][3][4].

Amortized analysis looks at the total time spent by all operations in a sequence and spreads the cost of the occasional expensive operation over the many cheap ones, so the average (amortized) cost per operation remains low【1】【3】.

Picking the largest‑value coin first can be suboptimal for some coin systems; for example, with coins {1, 3, 4} and target 6 the greedy choice 4 + 1 + 1 uses three coins, while the optimal solution 3 + 3 uses only two [1].  The problem is resolved by solving the coin‑change problem with dynamic programming, which yields an optimal solution for any set of coin values [2].

A segment tree can be built to answer many queries besides plain sums, such as minimum and maximum queries, greatest‑common‑divisor queries, and bit‑wise operations (AND, OR, XOR) on a range【1】. In general it supports “sum, minimum and maximum queries and many other queries” beyond simple range‑sum processing【2】.

Both binary indexed trees and segment trees answer range‑sum queries in \(O(\log n)\) time, but a BIT is a simpler array‑based structure that only supports sum queries, while a segment tree is a more general binary tree that can handle sums, minima, maxima and many other range operations (and can be extended with lazy propagation) at the cost of higher memory usage and implementation complexity【1】【2】. You would pick a BIT when you need only fast sum queries and want a compact, easy‑to‑code solution; you would choose a segment tree when you need other types of range queries or range updates that a BIT cannot provide【2】.
